title: What lies below the waterline of sustainable AI skills · hancrafted
description: When a task you keep explaining should become a skill, how to write its description as the moment you'd need it, what goes into the skill and what stays in project context, and what a shared skill needs to stay right: an owner, a version, tests and a retirement date.

When to write one (1/3) Page 1 of 3 The third time is the signal Write a skill the third time, once you know what a good result looks like. 1st time: you learn what's needed Which depth? What goes on the label? Collect sediment sample: hold 2 m above the seabed… Session 1 · starts fresh Skill · empty · procedure card Title: Use when: 1. 2. 3. What is needed: depth? label? Session 1 · new context window > Take a sediment sample at site 4. ● Which depth should the robot hold? How should I label the sample? > Hold 2 m above the seabed. Label it with site, depth and time. 2nd time: you refine it Seal the tube, then label? Again: check the camera first, lower the arm slowly. Session 2 · starts fresh Skill · draft · procedure card Collect sediment sample Use when: 1. Hold the robot 2 m above the seabed. 2. Grab the mud. 2. Lower the arm slowly . 3. Label it. Good result = ? Session 2 · new context window > Take a sediment sample at site 5. ● Which depth should the robot hold? > 2 m, like last time. Check the camera first, lower the arm slowly, seal the tube. 3rd time: you write the skill Intact, sealed, labelled. Got it. Here it is, written down. Session 3 · starts fresh Skill · written · procedure card Collect sediment sample Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. 1 Hold the robot 2 m above the seabed. 2 Check the camera for loose sediment. 3 Lower the arm. 4 Identify what you collected. 5 Seal the core tube. 6 Label the sample. ✓ Good result: an intact core, sealed and labelled. collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md new file --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Takes a sediment core. Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- 1. Hold the robot 2 m above the seabed. 2. Check the camera for loose sediment. 3. Lower the arm. 4. Identify what you collected. 5. Seal the core tube. 6. Label the sample. Good result: an intact core, sealed and labelled. Written to a file, it is there in session 4. ( ) Counting is not enough. If you cannot check whether the result was good, the skill repeats a habit with great confidence. Did you know? This matches the rule of three from Fowler's Refactoring ( ) , a software engineering rule against generalising too early. In the story: Explain the sample, refine it, write the card. In Claude Code or Codex: each session starts fresh, so only what you write to a file carries over. ( )

When to write one (2/3) Page 2 of 3 Not every repeat deserves a skill A skill written too early locks in a procedure nobody has proven. Skill index SKILL.md names 47 skills 47 folders Rinse the dome rinse-camera-dome never tested Sample (old) sample-old Take sample v2 take-sample-v2 never tested Name the photo folders name-photo-folders Sediment, quick version sediment-quick Sample, Ana's way sample-like-ana Collect sediment sample at a new site collect-sediment-sample needed Sample, but faster sample-but-faster never tested Write Tuesday's weather note tuesday-weather-note Clean the arm (maybe) clean-arm-maybe never tested Collect sediment sample (copy) collect-sediment-sample-copy Log depth (draft) log-depth-draft never tested Crew coffee order crew-coffee-order Check the winch, again check-winch-again Sample v3 (try this) sample-v3 never tested Label the cores, alt label-cores-alt Dive log, short form dive-log-short Before you write a skill Does the task repeat ? Does it have rules ? Does a mistake cost something? No to all three? Leave it in the chat. No to all three? Leave it in the prompt: no new SKILL.md . A practical filter, not a published test. After the check: 5 skills. Why check: every skill has a price. One more thing to keep right, and one more description in the skill index the AI reads every time. ( ) In the story: A manual stuffed with thin cards buries the one you need. Did you know? YAGNI: build a thing when you need it, not when you foresee it ( ) Knuth: premature optimisation is "the root of all evil", a rule about timing ( )

When to write one (3/3) Page 3 of 3 Write it from a good run Turn a run that worked into a skill: from your own notes, or by asking the AI to write it up. From an AI interview one day, from the run to the skill 2 m 1 A run that worked ( ) today's dive went well You did the task with the AI, giving context and corrections along the way. A session in the coding agent, not a guess from general knowledge. 2 The AI interviews you ( ) before evening, the pilot asks It asks for your intent, not only the steps. Why that depth? Why that order? What would have counted as failure? > Turn this conversation into a skill. With Anthropic's skill-creator, it reads the conversation first, then asks: Why that depth? Why that order? context window: full 3 The AI writes the skill he writes the card while he still knows In the same conversation, while the whole run is still in its context window. The skill it writes, below. The SKILL.md it writes, below. Nice to meet you. context window: empty 4 The next conversation starts fresh next morning he has forgotten the dive; the card hangs on the wall The run is forgotten. The skill is not. A new session opens with an empty context window; collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md is still on disk. 12 Mar 19 Mar 26 Mar From your own notes your logbook pages from earlier dives Notes from earlier runs, written up into the same skill. Or run the task with no skill loaded, then draft a SKILL.md from the transcript ( ) . Asking the AI to interview you works here too. → ↓ Skill Collect sediment sample 1 Hold the robot 2 m above the seabed. Why: closer, the thrusters stir up the mud. 2 Lower the arm slowly, push the corer in. 3 Label the core before storing. Why: unlabelled cores get mixed up. Failed if: core under 30 cm, or no depth logged. collect-sediment-sample/SKILL.md --- name: collect-sediment-sample description: Takes a sediment core. Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed. --- 1. Hold 2 m above the seabed. Why: closer stirs up the mud. 2. Lower the arm, push the corer in. 3. Label the core before storing. Failed if: core under 30 cm, or no depth logged. 1 First step: pick one task you've explained three times, and turn a good run of it into a skill. In the story: Your logbook pages, or the pilot's evening interview about today's good dive.

The third time is the signal When to write a skill: Fowler's rule of three "The first time you do something, you just do it. The second time you do something similar, you wince at the duplication, but you do the duplication thing anyway. The third time you do something similar, you refactor." 1 It is a heuristic, not a measured result. The credit to Don Roberts is in the 1999 book, which the research could not read. Sources (1) Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code (1997 slides) ( opens in a new tab ) pdfs.semanticscholar.org The model as a new employee: why the rule of thumb holds Anthropic tells the writer to think of Claude as "a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows", and to show a prompt to a colleague with minimal context 1 . Anthropic Engineering calls building a skill "like putting together an onboarding guide for a new hire" 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Prompting best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Anthropic Engineering, Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Where the model is not like a person each is backed by a source, but listing them as the breaks is a synthesis: sessions start fresh, so only written files carry over 1 ; rules in a file are "context, not enforced configuration" 1 ; newer models read instructions more literally 2 ; the same words read differently by model 2 ; assistants drift toward agreeing with the user 3 . Sources (3) Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com OpenAI, GPT-4.1 Prompting Guide ( opens in a new tab ) developers.openai.com Sharma et al., Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Not every repeat deserves a skill Skills written too early: Knuth on premature optimisation "We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%" 1 . His reason is a cost, and the same paper calls ignoring efficiency in the small "an overreaction", so it is a rule about timing and measurement. The quotes were not checked against the original (the ACM page returned 403). Sources (1) Knuth, Structured Programming with go to Statements ( opens in a new tab ) dl.acm.org Skills nobody needs yet: YAGNI, and what it does not cover "Always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you need them" 1 . Fowler counts four costs of a presumptive feature (build, delay, carry, repair) and says YAGNI does not apply to effort to make software easier to modify 2 . Sources (2) Jeffries, You're NOT gonna need it! ( opens in a new tab ) ronjeffries.com Fowler, Yagni ( opens in a new tab ) martinfowler.com A crowded skill index costs the AI too by default every skill's description is loaded on every turn, unless the skill is user-only, and Claude Code and Codex cap or shorten the skill listing, so a crowded index can shorten or drop descriptions 1 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com OpenAI, Build skills (Codex docs) ( opens in a new tab ) learn.chatgpt.com

Write it from a good run Write the skill from a real run the standard advises: "Complete a real task in conversation with an agent, providing context, corrections, and preferences along the way. Then extract the reusable pattern into a skill." A skill an LLM writes from general knowledge alone yields "vague, generic procedures" 1 . Sources (1) Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io The agent can interview you Anthropic's skill-creator checks the current conversation for a workflow the user wants to capture, extracts answers from it first, then interviews the user to fill gaps 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, skill-creator SKILL.md ( opens in a new tab ) github.com Run the task without a skill first: Google's route Day 3 suggests asking your most experienced practitioner to "narrate three workflows they do regularly", picking the most repeated one, running the prompts without any skill loaded, and drafting a SKILL.md from the transcript. It closes with "Resist the urge to let an LLM generate fifty skills on day one." 1 This agrees with the standard's advice to extract from a real run. It is Google's vendor guidance, not a measured result. Sources (1) Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:31 You are the captain Imagine you work with an AI model that is brilliant at its job, the most capable colleague you have. I will give it a picture, because we need one all the way down: you are the captain of a coastal research project, and the model is your pilot of ten years, who steers a diving robot on a cable from the control room on deck while you decide where the project goes next. 0:31 – 0:53 One settled condition Your pilot has one condition, and it never changes. He forms no new memories overnight, but he keeps everything he ever learnt as a pilot, every rule of the trade. That is an AI model: what it learnt in training stays, and what you told it in yesterday's conversation is gone.

What a skill is 0:00 – 0:23 Surface first We are still at the surface, so before we ask when to write a skill, let's see what a skill is made of. I'll use the words your chat app uses, and if you work with a coding agent, some Slides have a second view that shows you the files behind each part. 0:23 – 0:39 The mechanics, plainly I want to be exact about how a skill gets loaded, because everything later depends on it. So I say first what the AI really does, and use the dive only to make it easier to picture.

When to write one 0:00 – 0:14 Sunlight We are one level down, in the sunlit zone. Here we decide two things: when a task deserves a skill at all, and how to describe it so the model actually picks it. 0:14 – 0:31 Borrowed principles From here on I borrow principles from engineering, information architecture and UX, and they all lean on one idea: what works for people also works for AI. I say that as a strong rule of thumb, not as a law. 0:31 – 0:52 Why a rule of thumb It holds because the model acts only on what you hand it, like a capable newcomer on their first day. It is only a rule of thumb because there are places where it breaks, and I've put those in the notes on the next Slide for you to read.

The third time is the signal 0:00 – 0:27 Three tries So when does a task become a skill? Think about what you learn each time you explain it to the model. The first time you find out what is needed at all, the second time you tighten it, and by the third time you can tell what a good result looks like, which is the moment you know what you would be writing down. 0:27 – 0:42 Not only repetition But counting is not enough. If you cannot check whether the result was good, you are not capturing a procedure, you are copying a habit, and the skill will repeat your habit with great confidence. 0:42 – 1:03 Did you know Software engineers arrived at this the same way, long before any AI tool: they call it the rule of three, from Fowler's Refactoring, a rule against generalising too early. I'll leave the exact wording in the notes, because the point here is only that people got there first.

Not every repeat deserves a skill 0:00 – 0:13 Too early Now the opposite danger. If you write the skill after the first run, you freeze a guess, and a procedure nobody has proven now carries the authority of a skill. 0:13 – 0:33 A thin card has a price And every quick skill has a price. It is one more thing to keep right and one more line in an index that only grows, so picture a manual stuffed with thin cards, several of them never tested, until the one you need is buried in the middle. 0:33 – 0:54 Three questions So before you write a skill, ask three questions. Does the task repeat, does it have rules, and does a mistake cost something? If the answer is no to all three, leave it in the chat. This check is mine, a practical filter I use, not a published test.

Write it from a good run 0:00 – 0:21 Two starting points Say it is the third time and you are ready to write the skill. There are two good places to start: your own notes from earlier runs, the logbook pages of earlier dives, or a run with the AI that has just gone well, today's dive, while it is fresh. 0:21 – 0:43 Capture the why With the fresh run, ask the AI to interview you before it writes anything: why that depth, why that order, what would have counted as failure. You want the skill to hold your intent and not only the steps, because steps without the why break the first time the situation changes. 0:43 – 1:15 While he still knows Then let it write the skill in the same conversation, while the whole run is still in its context window. Tomorrow it will have forgotten, and that is the condition we started with. So that is your first step: pick one task you've explained three times, and turn a good run of it into a skill. In a coding agent, that is one sentence: ask it to turn this conversation into a skill.

The description 0:00 – 0:12 The label decides We are still in sunlight, and this is the part most people skip. A skill the model never picks helps nobody, so the description matters more than the instructions. 0:12 – 0:26 Name, description Before the model opens a skill, it sees two lines: the name and the description. That is all the index holds, and it is all the model has to decide with.

What context goes inside 0:00 – 0:13 Twilight Deeper now, into the twilight zone, where the light is dim. The skill is written and described, and the question is what context goes into it and what stays beside it. 0:13 – 0:28 A decision, not a law I want to be careful with the word rule here. Keeping the procedure apart from project details is a design decision with trade-offs on both sides, so I'll show you the trade-offs and you decide.

What context stays beside 0:00 – 0:15 Beside, not inside Now the other home: project details that stay outside the skill, in project files it reads when it runs. The procedure goes inside, and whatever changes from one project to the next stays beside. 0:15 – 0:29 Where it gets shared And who uses the skill decides how much care it needs. A skill for your own use can be loose, and a skill a colleague runs needs more, which sets up the next Section.

Sharing it 0:00 – 0:10 Midnight Now we are in deep water, the midnight zone. Everything so far was for you, so what changes when a colleague runs your skill? 0:10 – 0:22 Three jobs Three jobs wait down here. Give the skill an owner and a version, decide who looks after the shared library, and test that the skill actually helps.

Keeping it alive 0:00 – 0:09 The Abyss This is the deepest zone, the abyss, months later. Writing the skill was quick, and keeping it right is the work. 0:09 – 0:20 Nobody sees it Most people stop at the first good run, and the part below it gets little attention, which is why I want to spend three Slides here.
